cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK I
Athena comes to Ithaca;\nTelemachus resolves to seek his father.
Tell me the man, Muse —\nthe man of many turnings,
who was driven wandering far, once he had sacked\nTroy’s holy citadel:
many were the cities of men he saw,\nand he learned their minds,
many the griefs he suffered at heart\non the open sea,
striving to win his own life\nand his companions’ homecoming.
Even so he could not save them,\nhard though he strove:
they perished by their own recklessness,
fools, who ate the cattle\nof Helios Hyperion,
and the god took from them\ntheir day of homecoming.
Begin where you will, goddess, daughter of Zeus —\ntell us, too, the tale.
By then all the others,\nall who had escaped sheer ruin,
were home, safely past the war\nand past the sea.
Him alone — aching for homecoming\nand his wife —
the queenly nymph Calypso,\nshining among goddesses, held back
in her hollow caves,\nhungry to make him her husband.
But when the year came,\nin the wheeling round of seasons,
in which the gods had spun the thread\nof his return home to Ithaca —
not even there was he free of trials,\neven among his own.
And the gods pitied him, all but Poseidon:\nhe raged without rest
against godlike Odysseus,\nuntil the day he reached his own land.
But now Poseidon was gone\namong the far-off Ethiopians —
the Ethiopians, sundered in two,\nremotest of mankind,
half where Hyperion sets\nand half where he rises —
to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams,\nand there he sat at the feast, delighting.
But the other gods were gathered together\nin the halls of Olympian Zeus,
